      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

AI-generated 'FULLY FIXED' PowerShell AD enumeration writing AD_Report.html AIReconnaissance High
Hunts creation of the AD_Report.html inventory artifact by PowerShell, the distinctive output file of the vibe-coded 'AD Information Gathering' script Huntress observed. AD_Report.html is a bespoke, non-standard filename produced only by this enumeration tool, making its creation a high-fidelity discovery signal. Rationale: AD_Report.html is an article-specific bespoke filename (the script's own success-measure artifact); pairing it with a PowerShell writer removes any residual noise. Cross-checked against the Huntress write-up which names the artifact and the script title. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vibe-coded-powershell-script-active-directory/
ATT&CKT1087.002 T1018 T1482 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin's own AD documentation/reporting script that coincidentally names its output AD_Report.html
  • Commercial AD auditing tools (e.g. some PingCastle/ADRecon wrappers) if re-templated to that filename
  • A pentest/red-team engagement reusing the same public script
  • Security-team baselining exercise generating an AD inventory report
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADComputer","nltest","DirectorySearcher")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain; confirm the script matches the 'AD Information Gathering' / cascading-fallback profile and whether it ran from C:\ProgramData. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the executing account, and kill the RDP session it originated from; the pre-compromised credential should be reset domain-wide. 3) Hunt: look on the same host for s5cmd.exe and SharpShares.exe execution and a newly created staging directory of AD CSV exports within the surrounding 60 minutes.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "AD_Report.html"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where TargetFileName =~ "AD_Report.html"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharpShares network-share enumeration binary staged in C:\ProgramData AIReconnaissance High
Hunts execution of SharpShares, the C#-based network share enumeration utility Huntress saw deployed ~30 minutes after AD enumeration to locate user-accessible data repositories. Matches on the binary name and its embedded original-filename metadata so a simple rename doesn't evade, with a C:\ProgramData staging fallback. Rationale: SharpShares is explicitly named in the article as the share-enumeration tool; matching FileName plus ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName defeats trivial rename, and the C:\ProgramData staging path mirrors the observed tradecraft. Corroborated by the Huntress blog naming SharpShares and s5cmd. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/vibe-coded-malware-ai-powershell/
ATT&CKT1135 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team/pentest engagement running SharpShares
  • Internal share-inventory/audit script that shells out to SharpShares
  • A file-server migration project enumerating shares
  • Security researcher testing the tool in a lab VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","explorer.exe") and (FolderPath startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\" or FolderPath startswith "C:\\Users\\Public\\" or FolderPath startswith "C:\\Windows\\Temp\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing account and whether the parent chain traces to an RDP-launched shell in C:\ProgramData; capture the SHA256 and command line. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the session, and disable the account; treat any share paths in the command line as targeted collection scope. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for AD_Report.html creation, s5cmd cloud egress, and archive creation (.zip/.7z) of the enumerated CSVs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "SharpShares.exe"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "SharpShares.exe"
    or (FolderPath startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\" and ProcessCommandLine has "shares" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ldap","--filter","--outfile","/ldap","/outfile"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\SharpShares.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

s5cmd bulk cloud-storage exfiltration tool executed from C:\ProgramData AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of s5cmd — a legitimate high-throughput S3/object-storage transfer utility — with copy/sync arguments, as used in the final exfiltration stage of the Huntress-reported AD theft. s5cmd is not a normal endpoint binary on a domain-joined server, so its execution with cp/sync/s3:// arguments is a strong exfil signal. Rationale: s5cmd is explicitly named as the bulk transfer/exfil tool; requiring cp/sync/s3:// arguments keeps it aligned to the exfiltration action rather than a benign presence. Corroborated by the Huntress write-up which names s5cmd for the exfil stage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://cyberpress.org/ai-coded-vibe-coding-map-active-directory/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DevOps/backup job legitimately using s5cmd to push to S3
  • Data-lake or log-shipping automation that bundles s5cmd
  • An admin manually testing S3 connectivity from a jump server
  • Cloud migration tooling copying datasets to object storage
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("jenkins.exe","agent.exe","gitlab-runner.exe") or AccountName startswith "svc-" or AccountName startswith "svc_")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the s5cmd command line for the destination bucket/endpoint and credentials source; determine what files/archive were being pushed and from which staging directory. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke the AWS/S3 access keys used, and block the destination endpoint at egress; preserve the archive for scoping. 3) Hunt: correlate the exact same host/account back to SharpShares, AD_Report.html, and the AD CSV export directory to reconstruct the collection set, and check for any prior s5cmd runs indicating repeated exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "s5cmd.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "s5cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cp","sync","mv","s3://","--endpoint-url")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\s5cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("s3://","sync"," cp ","--endpoint-url")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: s5cmd Cloud Object-Storage Transfer Execution (Exfiltration)
id: 9a3d1f77-4e21-4c0b-b6d8-2f7c5a9e1b30
description: Detects s5cmd executed with copy/sync/s3 arguments, used for bulk exfiltration to object storage in the Huntress vibe-coded AD attack.
references:
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory
author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:
  category: process_creation

detection:
  selection_img:
    - Image|endswith: '\s5cmd.exe'
    - OriginalFileName: 's5cmd.exe'
  selection_args:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 's3://'
      - 'sync'
      - '--endpoint-url'
  condition: selection_img and selection_args
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\s5cmd.exe OR *\\S5cmd.exe OR *\\S5CMD.EXE) OR @OriginalFileName:s5cmd.exe) @CommandLine:(*s3\://* OR *sync* OR *cp* OR *--endpoint-url*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\s5cmd\.exe$/i
| regex("(s3://|--endpoint-url|sync|\\bcp\\b|\\bmv\\b)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="s5cmd.exe" OR Processes.original_file_name="s5cmd.exe") (Processes.process="*cp*" OR Processes.process="*sync*" OR Processes.process="*mv*" OR Processes.process="*s3://*" OR Processes.process="*--endpoint-url*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="s5cmd.exe" OR Processes.original_file_name="s5cmd.exe") (Processes.process="*cp*" OR Processes.process="*sync*" OR Processes.process="*mv*" OR Processes.process="*s3://*" OR Processes.process="*--endpoint-url*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Executable in C:\ProgramData root launched within an RDP session (attacker tool staging) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts binaries executed directly from the C:\ProgramData\ root correlated with a RemoteInteractive (RDP) logon on the same host — the exact tool-staging pattern Huntress observed after the attacker RDP'd in with pre-compromised credentials. C:\ProgramData root (not a vendor subfolder) is an unusual home for a running EXE, and pairing it with an RDP session distinguishes hands-on-keyboard staging from legitimate installers. Rationale: The article states tools were staged in C:\ProgramData\ after RDP access with pre-compromised creds; anchoring on EXEs directly in the ProgramData root (regex-excluding vendor subfolders) plus a RemoteInteractive logon correlation captures the hands-on staging without the noise of legit software in ProgramData subfolders. Cross-checked with the Huntress blog describing RDP entry and ProgramData staging. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attacker-uses-suspected-ai-generated.html
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1074.001 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate installer that briefly drops and runs a bootstrap EXE at the ProgramData root during an admin RDP session
  • RMM/monitoring agents that self-update from C:\ProgramData while an admin is remoted in
  • An admin manually running a portable diagnostic tool copied to ProgramData over RDP
  • Antivirus/EDR components that stage temporary executables at the ProgramData root
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","services.exe") or FileName in~ ("setup.exe","update.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the EXE (SHA256, signer, command line) and the RDP source IP/account from the join; determine whether the binary is s5cmd/SharpShares/PowerShell-related or otherwise unsigned/unknown. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the RDP session, and disable + reset the pre-compromised account across the domain; block the source IP at the RDP gateway. 3) Hunt: sweep the domain for the same source IP hitting RDP on other servers, and on this host for AD_Report.html, SharpShares, s5cmd, and an AD-export staging directory created in the same session window.
let RdpLogons = DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LogonType == "RemoteInteractive"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project RdpTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, RdpUser = AccountName, RemoteIP;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)^C:\\ProgramData\\[^\\]+\.exe$"
| join kind=inner RdpLogons on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (RdpTime .. RdpTime + 12h)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, RdpTime, RdpUser, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let Rdp = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 10
| project RdpTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, RdpUser = TargetUserName, IpAddress;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^C:\\ProgramData\\[^\\]+\.exe$"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner Rdp on Computer

Misconfigured Server Reveals Three Evilginx Phishing Operations Targeting Microsoft 365

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An attacker running a live Microsoft 365 phishing operation left a Python web server listening on a public port with directory listing switched on. The command that did it:&nbsp;python3 -m http.server 8080, was still sitting in the readable&nbsp;.bash_history. From that one lapse, French security firm&nbsp;Lexfo&nbsp;lifted the operator's entire toolkit and pivoted through it to two more

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Stolen M365 session token refresh — same account, many IPs, non-interactive (token aging) · Network connections to article IPs / domains

M365 AiTM sign-in from Evilginx phishing infrastructure IPs (codemado / mail-argenta) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins whose source IP is one of the four Evilginx/SimpleHelp hosts Lexfo pulled from the misconfigured Budapest server. In an AiTM proxy the victim's live login is relayed through the operator's server, so the Microsoft-side sign-in shows the proxy IP, not the victim's — a direct, high-fidelity IOC pivot. Rationale: Uses the four second-source-corroborated infra IPs (185.163.204.7 hosted both the Evilginx proxy and SimpleHelp console) as direct sign-in-source IOCs; AiTM relays the real login so the Microsoft sign-in carries the proxy IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1557 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher or IR team logging into a honeypot/decoy tenant from the same VPS range
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling that authenticates test accounts through a proxy
  • Shared-hosting IP reassignment months later to a benign SaaS the org legitimately uses
  • A pentest engagement deliberately routing M365 auth through a rented Budapest VPS
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the AccountUpn actually authenticated and pull the full sign-in row — ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, resource. Cross-check whether the same user signed in from a normal IP minutes before/after (AiTM proxy relay). Step 2 (contain): revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-registration of MFA. Block the four IPs at Conditional Access / firewall. Step 3 (hunt): search all sign-ins from these IPs across every account, then hunt for post-compromise mailbox rules, OAuth app consents, and token refreshes from unrelated geos on the affected accounts.

| order by Timestamp desc

| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft 365 device-code-flow phishing sign-in (black-queen / saroula01) AIExploitation High
Hunts Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth device code flow — the mechanism saroula01's black-queen fork abuses: a genuine device code wrapped in an Authenticator-themed lure, with the victim authorizing the attacker's session on real Microsoft infrastructure. Device code flow is rare in most orgs, so surfacing it (especially first-time-per-user and toward the Microsoft Authentication Broker app) is high-signal. Rationale: Device code flow is the exact mechanism the article says black-queen uses (real device code + genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin, so FIDO2/passkey origin binding does not help); Microsoft's Storm-2372 advisory confirms the same technique and the Microsoft Authentication Broker client-ID pivot for refresh-token/device-registration abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://www.aha.org/h-isac-white-reports/2025-02-14-h-isac-tlp-white-threat-bulletin-storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code auth on genuinely input-constrained hardware (conference-room displays, IoT, some CLI tools like az login --use-device-code)
  • Developers using 'az login --use-device-code' or PowerShell Device Login on headless build agents
  • Smart-TV / Apple TV / streaming-stick enrollment of a corporate Teams Rooms account
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that still rely on device code grant
Suppression filter
| where not(Apps has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and array_length(IPs) == 1)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each surfaced UPN, check whether device code flow is expected for that user/device class; inspect the target app (flag Microsoft Authentication Broker / device registration service — per Storm-2372 that path leads to PRT theft) and the IP/geo of the completing sign-in. Step 2 (contain): revoke sessions and refresh tokens for the user, disable device code flow via a Conditional Access authentication-flow policy, and review/remove any attacker-registered devices in Entra ID. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the same IPs and app IDs across all accounts, review non-interactive refresh activity, and check for newly joined/registered devices and mailbox exfil rules on affected identities.

| extend ProcDetails = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where ProcDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Apps=make_set(Application,10), Countries=make_set(Country,10) by AccountUpn
| order by FirstSeen desc
SigninLogs

| order by FirstSeen desc

Stolen M365 session token refresh — same account, many IPs, non-interactive (token aging) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the article's described behaviour of operators refreshing stolen tokens as they age out — the same corporate mailbox captured repeatedly from different IPs, and black-queen's autoRefresh tokens re-refreshed up to 25 times. Detects a single account accruing an abnormal number of distinct source IPs on non-interactive (refresh-token) sign-ins in a short window. Rationale: Directly models the article's 'repeated captures of the same accounts from different IPs' and autoRefresh tokens refreshed up to 25 times; non-interactive + high distinct-IP fan-out per account isolates token replay from normal user roaming. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile users roaming across carrier/Wi-Fi networks generating many refresh IPs
  • Corporate VPN or SASE egress that rotates public IPs per session
  • Background Office/Outlook/Teams token refreshes across multiple devices for one power user
  • Shared service/kiosk account legitimately used from many locations
Suppression filter
| where not(Apps has_any ("Microsoft VPN Client","Microsoft Intune") )
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): review the IP/geo/ASN spread and app mix for the flagged account — legitimate roaming clusters by carrier/VPN ASN, whereas token theft shows unrelated hosting/VPS ASNs. Correlate against any interactive AiTM or device-code sign-in for the same user. Step 2 (contain): revoke all refresh tokens and sessions, reset credentials, and apply a short sign-in frequency + CAE-capable Conditional Access policy so a reset actually invalidates stolen tokens. Step 3 (hunt): enumerate mailbox rules, OAuth consents, and forwarding added during the window; check whether any of the fan-out IPs overlap the known Evilginx infra IPs and pivot to other victims.

| where DistinctIPs >= 5   // >=5 distinct refresh-token source IPs/day for one account = token-replay fan-out
| order by DistinctIPs desc

| where DistinctIPs >= 5   // >=5 distinct refresh-token source IPs/day for one account = token-replay fan-out

Endpoint connections to Evilginx phishing landing domains (picis.net / romnor.ca) AIDelivery High
Hunts managed endpoints resolving or connecting to the three phishing domains tied to the operations — picis[.]net and romnor[.]ca (plus queeenspropertyservices[.]ca) — which fronted the Evilginx AiTM proxies and their rotating wildcard subdomains. A hit means a user reached the phishing landing page and is a candidate victim before/at credential capture. Rationale: picis[.]net and romnor[.]ca are named as the two phishing domains and queeenspropertyservices[.]ca is in the IOC bundle; picis[.]net was still provisioning new subdomains as late as May 2026, so wildcard matching catches rotating hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually detonating the phishing URL from a corporate host during triage
  • Threat-intel sandbox/crawler VM resolving the domains for enrichment
  • URL-reputation or email-security appliance pre-fetching links from a managed endpoint
  • Domain later parked/reassigned to a benign owner after takedown, generating benign lookups
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the user and process that made the request (browser vs automated tool) and whether a sign-in followed on the same identity shortly after (candidate AiTM capture). Step 2 (contain): sinkhole/block the three domains and their wildcards at DNS/proxy, and if the user authenticated, revoke sessions + reset credentials + re-register MFA. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the resolved IPs (cross-check the four Evilginx infra IPs), search email/Safe Links telemetry for the delivering message and other recipients, and check for subsequent device-code or token-refresh anomalies on the affected account.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

iCagenda and Balbooa Forms Joomla Flaws Reportedly Exploited as Zero-Days

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 4 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added two maximum-severity security flaws impacting iCagenda and Balbooa extensions for Joomla to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of zero-day exploitation in the wild. The vulnerabilities, both rated 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system, are below - CVE-2026-48939 - A vulnerability in the

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] iCagenda 'Submit an Event' scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' in web logs (CVE-2026-48939)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PHP web shell written to Joomla iCagenda/Balbooa upload folders (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] HTTP request to planted PHP shell under iCagenda/Balbooa upload paths (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
iCagenda 'Submit an Event' scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' in web logs (CVE-2026-48939) AIDelivery High
Hunts web-server access logs for the automated exploitation scanner that identifies itself with the User-Agent 'icagenda-batch/1.0', the exact tool mySites.guru observed grabbing a token and POSTing a malicious upload to the iCagenda Submit-an-Event endpoint since 15 June 2026. This UA is not a legitimate browser, crawler or monitoring agent, so any hit is a direct exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-48939. Rationale: Uses the literal exploitation scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' named by mySites.guru and reproduced in the article; a non-browser UA string this specific has effectively zero legitimate use, making it alerting-grade on the first hit. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-actively-exploited-rce-flaws-in-joomla-extensions/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4rh3-rmh3-hv6h
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) deliberately fingerprinting iCagenda with a spoofed UA during an authorized scan
  • Security researcher / red-team replaying the PoC against a staging site
  • A monitoring probe an admin scripted using the same UA string to test their own patch
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the matched source IP(s) — confirm the sequence token GET -> POST to the iCagenda submit endpoint -> GET of a new .php under images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and, if a PHP file was fetched, take the site offline or WAF-block the attachments path immediately. 3) Hunt: list images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/ for any .php/.phtml files, diff the Joomla #__users table for new Super Admin accounts, and confirm iCagenda is on 4.0.8/3.9.15.

PHP web shell written to Joomla iCagenda/Balbooa upload folders (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a PHP-executable file inside the two upload directories these flaws write to — 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' and 'images/baforms/uploads' — which by design should only ever hold user-submitted images and documents. A .php/.phtml/.phar in either folder is the planted web shell mySites.guru flagged as the primary IOC for both CVEs. Rationale: Pins on the two exact upload paths (images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/, images/baforms/uploads) plus PHP-executable extensions — both vendors explicitly say these folders must never contain PHP, so any hit is the planted shell rather than a legit attachment. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://mysites.guru/blog/balbooa-forms-unauthenticated-file-upload-flaw/ • https://www.cycognito.com/blog/emerging-threat-cve-2026-56291-balbooa-forms-remote-code-execution-via-unauthenticated-file-upload/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Site migration/backup-restore tooling (Akeeba Kickstart, rsync) copying the whole webroot including an already-present benign file that happens to match
  • Admin manually placing a legitimate index.php as a directory-listing guard in the uploads folder
  • A previous compromise remediation that quarantined-in-place rather than deleting, retriggering on file rename
  • Antivirus renaming a detected file to .php.quarantine style names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("kickstart.php","restore.php") and not (FolderPath has "backup" or FolderPath has "tmp\\install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file — decode any eval/base64/assert/system calls, note the SHA256 and the InitiatingProcess (should be the web server / php-fpm). 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the file, WAF-block direct requests to the two upload paths, and isolate the host if the shell was already accessed. 3) Hunt: pull web logs for GET requests to that filename (attacker interaction), search for new Joomla Super Admin accounts and other recently-modified PHP files across the webroot, and confirm iCagenda>=4.0.8/3.9.15 and Balbooa Forms>=2.4.1.
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed") | where FileName has_any (".php",".phtml",".phar",".php5") | where (FolderPath has "icagenda" and FolderPath has "attachments") or (FolderPath has "baforms" and FolderPath has "uploads") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileName has_any (".php",".phtml",".phar",".php5") | where (TargetFilePath has "icagenda" and TargetFilePath has "attachments") or (TargetFilePath has "baforms" and TargetFilePath has "uploads") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256 | sort by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP request to planted PHP shell under iCagenda/Balbooa upload paths (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291) AICommand & Control High
Detects the attacker fetching/executing the planted web shell — a GET/POST to a .php file located under 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' or 'images/baforms/uploads' in web-server access logs. mySites.guru observed the scanner 'fetched the planted shell at the exact path the component writes attachments to', and requests to a PHP file in a media-upload directory are inherently anomalous. Rationale: Combines the two literal upload URI paths from both advisories with a '.php' request — a PHP file being requested from a media-attachment directory is the web-shell-interaction signal, distinct from the file-drop and the scanner-UA pivots. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://mysites.guru/blog/balbooa-forms-unauthenticated-file-upload-flaw/ • https://www.securityweek.com/organizations-warned-of-exploited-joomla-extension-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate index.php directory-index guard in the uploads folder being requested by a crawler
  • Internal DAST/WAF validation scan probing the patched path and receiving a 404 (filter on scStatus==200 to cut these)
  • Uptime monitor configured to hit a known-good health-check PHP under a media path
Suppression filter
| where Status == 200
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — a 200 to a .php in these folders means the shell executed; capture the source IP, requested filename and any query-string commands. 2) Contain: block the source IP and the upload path at the WAF, then delete the referenced PHP file from disk and isolate the web host. 3) Hunt: correlate the filename back to the DeviceFileEvents/FileWritten drop, review Joomla admin-user changes and outbound connections from the web host in the same window, and verify both extensions are patched.
